fields.title: Migrations: why a field can be expensive
fields.keyTakeaway: The cost of a data change is determined not by the size of the schema edit, but by the volume of accumulated data and the number of places reading that structure.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: You ask to add a "date of birth" field to the profile. Estimate: half a day. You ask to make the "phone" field mandatory. Estimate: a week, and a conversation about "what to do with old ones." The difference looks disproportionate until you understand what a [[migration|migration]] consists of.
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Failing to understand migration costs causes two kinds of damage. A PM promises a client a data model change by a specific date, not knowing it requires a maintenance window. And a PM rejects cheap changes because all changes seem equally scary to them. The second is quieter and more harmful—it does not cause a failure, it simply keeps the product from moving forward.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: A migration is a schema change combined with already accumulated data. Three parts, and the second one is usually expensive.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Change the schema.** Fast on its own. Adding a [[nullable|nullable]] column in a modern relational database takes seconds regardless of table size.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Bring existing data into compliance.** This is where everything happens. The new field is empty for millions of old records. If it must be filled, you need a [[backfill|backfill]]—going through all records and calculating the value. For eight million orders, this means hours of work, database load, and the risk that something breaks in the middle.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **Change the code that works with it.** Including the old version of the app code that is on users' phones and won't update tomorrow.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/0/2: Schema changes instantly, old records can be empty
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/1/2: Requires backfill and a decision on what to write into old records
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/2/2: Lives in two versions until all clients update
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/3/2: Data must be converted, some may fail to convert
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/rows/5/2: Logic changes wherever the relationship is read
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: The last row is the exact reason why "splitting an order with a neighbor" took three weeks.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Three real cases from the same database.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *«Add a comment to an order».* Optional text. Half a day, mostly for the interface.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: *«Make the phone number mandatory».* 340 thousand old users do not have a phone. You cannot just declare the field mandatory—the database will refuse. Solution: the field remains optional in the schema, mandatory status is checked in the app upon the next login, and old users fill it in gradually. A week, and half of it is product decisions on where and how to ask.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: *«One order to multiple addresses».* Currently, an order has one address. You need to turn one-to-many into many-to-many via order items. Everything is affected: checkout, payment, fulfillment, courier app, reporting. Three weeks, and that is an honest estimate.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: The estimates above are for a single database of a reasonable size. In a distributed system with multiple services, each having its own database, a migration turns into a coordinated change of several contracts, and the cost order grows. In addition, some changes cannot be performed without [[downtime|downtime]]—they are scheduled for the night and coordinated with the business.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: The cost of a data change is determined not by the size of the schema edit, but by the volume of accumulated data and the number of places reading that structure.
